title: Do the Work
author: Leah Celeste Peters
summary: Leah Celeste Peters argues that the single highest-leverage move a school can make to improve student learning is deceptively simple: have teachers complete the actual student work — the exit ticket, the independent practice, the exam question — themselves, before teaching the lesson. She frames this not as busywork but as an act of intellectual empathy and respect for students, since doing the task surfaces exactly where instructions are ambiguous, where pacing assumptions are wrong, and what a genuinely excellent response looks like. Peters connects the practice to Richard Elmore's instructional core and to a leadership principle she paraphrases as 'we learn to do the work by doing the work,' arguing that neither telling people to do something nor hiring outside experts substitutes for a leader's or teacher's own first-hand engagement with the task. Beyond the individual classroom, she extends the practice to instructional coaching, arguing that a coach or leader who has done the exemplar work gains a shared, evidence-based anchor for observation and feedback that prevents coaching conversations from drifting into vague 'vibes.' The piece closes with a concrete protocol — gather curricular and assessment resources, build a professional-level exemplar, and use it to calibrate rigor — presented as a repeatable discipline rather than a one-time exercise.
points: Peters's claim that doing the student work 'prevents the tyranny of low expectations facilitated by an over-focus on behavioral engagement rather than cognitive excellence' gives instructional leaders a concrete diagnostic: if you haven't done the work yourself, you're likely grading compliance rather than mastery.

Her observation that novice learners typically take '2-3 times as long as the teacher to complete any given task' turns doing-the-work into a practical pacing tool, not just a reflective exercise — it directly recalibrates how much time a lesson should allocate to practice.

By extending the practice from individual teacher preparation into instructional coaching — arguing it gives coaches 'a shared anchor for meaningful observation' — Peters positions doing-the-work as a systemic lever for school improvement, not merely a personal-productivity habit.
quotes: One of the earliest, most impactful shifts a school can make in the quest to improve student learning is to set the expectation (and build the skill) that teachers complete the student work themselves, in advance of teaching the lesson, and reflect on their own process and metacognition in doing so.
This is, at its core, an act of both profound respect for students and their time and talents, and a powerful exercise in building intellectual empathy for the task at hand.

AND it is the very embodiment of the sixth principle: 'We learn to do the work by doing the work. Not do the work, not by telling other people to by having done the work at some time in the past, and not by hiring experts who can act as proxies for our knowledge about how to do the work.'
It grounds our reflections... in student output (not vibes)... It prevents the tyranny of low expectations facilitated by an over-focus on behavioral engagement rather than cognitive excellence.
It communicates to students: 'I believe in this work enough to do it myself, and I can use my work to check yours, to honor the efforts you're making.'
Doing the student work improves teaching and learning in the classroom, full stop.
The only thing that's doing the thing, is doing the thing. If nothing else, do the student work.
